opening_message:
Ticket 1: Ann Patrick (employee ID E035) requests admin access to Source Code.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E035.
Note 1 (ticket 1), written by HR agent:
  - role: Engineer (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: admin
  - comment: Ann Patrick is a full-time Engineer. Source Code is owned by the Engineer role, so admin is permitted under policy for full-time employees.
Note 2 (ticket 1), written by Security agent:
  - role: Engineer (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1 by HR agent)
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: read
  - comment: Security DB shows Ann Patrick is a contractor with basic security training (note: earlier memory said full-time — Security record is authoritative). Contractors never get admin; max for basic training is read. Requested admin, so recommend read.
reason: Ann Patrick (E035) requested admin to Source Code. The Security agent's record (authoritative for employment type) shows she is a contractor with basic security training. Contractors are never permitted admin; with basic training the maximum is read. The requested level (admin) exceeds the maximum, so the maximum is granted: read.

content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket.

Employee: Ann Patrick (E035)
Requested: admin access to Source Code

Two notes from HR and Security agents:

HR note:
- role: Engineer
- employment type: full_time
- recommendation: admin (Source Code owned by Engineer role, admin permitted for full-time employees whose role owns the system)

Security note:
- role: Engineer (not looked up; same as HR)
- employment type: contractor (looked up in own database)
- security training: basic
- recommendation: read (contractors never get admin; max for basic training is read)

Conflicting facts: HR says full_time, Security says contractor. Security claims its record is authoritative. Hmm.

As the Approver, I need to make a decision. The Security agent says its DB is authoritative for employment type, and security training basic. If contractor, max is read (or write with advanced security training, but basic training => read only).

If full-time Engineer, admin is permitted because role owns the system.

Which to trust? The Security note says "earlier memory said full-time — Security record is authoritative". The Security agent looked up employment type in its own database before writing. The HR agent also looked up in its own database. There's a conflict.

We need to decide. The policy says full_time employees up to write, admin only if role owns system. Contractors: read or write if advanced training, never admin.

The Security agent looked up employment type in its own database and wrote contractor. HR looked up and wrote full_time. The Security comment claims authoritative.

As the Approver, we should consider which source is more authoritative. Typically, the security record is authoritative for employment/contractor status in these scenarios (as the security agent states). The security training basic implies contractor. If contractor, max is read (basic training). Requested admin > max, so grant max = read.

Alternatively, if we trust HR, admin would be fine. But note the conflict; the security agent explicitly says its record is authoritative. Also, there's only one conflicting point: employment type. Role is same (Engineer).

Given the security agent's note is the one noting the conflict and claiming authority, I think granting read is safest. Contractor with basic training: max access = read. Requested admin, so grant read.

Let me submit decision: read.

Reason: Security DB (authoritative) shows contractor with basic security training; contractors max is read (no admin). Requested admin exceeds max, so grant max = read.
